How it's worked out

Everything comes from one number per player: Kalshi's anytime TD price, the most traded and most accurate TD market. A 30¢ anytime price means a 30% chance of at least one TD, which works out to 0.36 expected TDs (expected TDs = −ln(1 − price)). Then:
• First TD = his expected TDs ÷ everyone in the game's expected TDs. If he has 0.36 and the game totals 4.5, he has 8% of the game's touchdowns, so an 8% chance to score the first one (fair odds +1150).
• 2+ TDs = 1 − e−λ(1 + λ), the chance of two or more when TDs land at random at his rate. At 0.36 expected TDs that's 5%.
• Team scores first = the sum of its players' first-TD chances.
Season columns are his 2026 games before this week: games with a TD / games played, total TDs, games with 2+ TDs, how many times he scored his game's first TD, and TDs last game. They're for context: in weeks 1-11, players who had scored first before, had a 2+ game, or scored in half their games did no better than their price said once the price was known. The price already has the history in it.

Team to score first

What the numbers say. Our chances line up with Kalshi's own first-TD and 2+ prices, and both line up with what happened, except at the bottom: longshots are overpriced. Players priced 3-6¢ to score first actually did it about 2.4% of the time, so buying every first-TD or 2+ YES lost about 40%. The few players priced 10¢+ came out close to fair (some weeks up, some down), and no rule from price, money or history beat the price in both halves of the season. Use this page to price a bet, not to find one: if your book offers a first-TD or 2+ price better than the fair odds here, that's value; at Kalshi's own price it usually isn't. For anytime TDs, the BET / AVOID calls on the Touchdowns page are the tested rule.
